Hon. E. M. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence) for the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) moved that the House go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the act respecting the construction of a Canadian National Railway line from the end of the China Clay branch to St. Remi d'Amherst in the province of Quebec, chapter fourteen of the statutes of 1924, and to provide that the compensation to be paid by the company in respect of the acquisition of an unencumbered title to the right of way and all prior construction thereon of the River Rouge Railway Company or the Rouge River Railway Company between China Clay and St. Remi d'Amherst, be determined by the Exchequer Court of Canada and shall be based on the value to the company of such right of way and prior construction, but shall not in any case exceed fourteen thousand dollars.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the House.
Motion agreed to.

I desire to direct the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) to the following statement which appears on the front page of the Toronto Globe of Wednesday, May 27, 1925:
Government to Occupy Ten Stories
The Dominion government has decided upon the centralization of its various Toronto offices in the new "Canadian National Building," to be erected at the northwest corner of King and Yonge streets.
Including the Canadian National Railways space, the Dominion government will take a lease of at least ten stories in the new building. The lower three will be used as railway offices, and the seven immediately above will be occupied by the Customs and Income Tax staff, Public Works, Labor department and Department of Agriculture officials.
The housing of these officials in the new skyscraper will have nothing to do with the ultimate erection of a customs house in Toronto wrhen, in the opinion of the government, the time is opportune for that course of action.

He might not at
the time refuse. He might assent and then while assenting fail to do it.
I really think the minister is looking for trouble when he words the section in this way. I do not think you can pass an act of that kind; I do not think you could enforce it if it were passed.

There may be a
little difficulty there but if my hon. friends think the provision is too wide-

I think it is altogether
too wide.

My hon. friends, of course can imagine a case where the inspector turned away to do something else and on returning found that although the man had assented-he had not refused-had failed to do as he was requested.

If a man is requested
to do a thing and does not do it it is a refusal no matter what he says. We have, probably, a good illustration in Holy Writ where a man said to his son "go work to-day in my vineyard" and he answered and said "I will not"; but aftc.ward he repented and went. And he came to the second and said likewise. And he answered and said, "I go, sir"; and went not. And he who said "I will not" and afterwards went was justified, while the other was condemned.
Mr, MOTHERWELL:	Will my hon.
friend move to substitute the word "refuses" for the word "fails?"
[Mr. Meighen.l

I will move that the
word "refuses" be substituted for the word "fails" in the second line.

I have no particular
business to be warning the minister, but I never saw legislation like that which is proposed here before. I will read the provision to hon. members; if they want to pass it all right. This is the way the law reads now:
Every person who obstructs any person charged with the enforcement of this act in entering any premises to make examination of dairy products* * * or who refuses to permit the making of any such examination, shall be liable to a penalty-
And so forth. That is reasonable. But listen to the wording of the section here:
Any person who obstructs an inspector in carrying out any of the provisions of this act-
It is all right so far. Let me continue:
-or who fails to give any such officer all reasonable assistance in his power-
And so on. Now, if a man is walking
along the street not in the least concerned, who is not even asked-there is a lot of assistance that is in bis power to give and he does not give it; Is he to be guilty of an offence and liable to be committed to gaol?

He would, in this case.
Mr. MEIGHE'N: In other words the man who drafted this provision does not know how to draft. The minister talks about the trouble he has experienced. He will never know what trouble is until somebody tries to enforce this section. He will know what trouble is then. Let us see further:
Any person who obstructs an inspector in carrying out any of the provisions of this act-
I do not object to that:
-or who fails to give any 6uch officer all reasonable assistance in his power, or to furnish him with any information he may reasonably require,
The middle feature is the worst, although the last one is bad too; it says here that if a man fails to do something he is a criminal. The fellow encountered on the street is just as liable as anybody else although he has not been asked to do anything. I could not make a suggestion as to how the section should be worded at the moment, but the minister will be well advised if he reserves this clause.

Of course, whether
this provision would be wise or the contrary will depend on the manner in which it is administered. Under the old act much

Dairy Industry Act
difficulty was experienced, because of having to just nail a man right down in order to prove anything. This provision has been made purposely wide so as to make it easier to prove our case and get a conviction; that is the avowed purpose of it. The provision would not look so extreme if my right hon. friend could picture the circumstances which call for it. Take a warehouse, as I pointed out a few moments ago, and the tenant or owner, as the case may be, refuses to give the necessary assistance to take out some parcels.

That is all right, but
the minister has not said "the owner or the man in charge." Surely the man down the street, who has nothing to do with the matter at all, is not expected to be hauled in off the street and told that he must take out boxes and that if he fails to do so he commits an offence.

My right hon.
friend has such a vivid imagination he can picture anything.

I am only citing an
extreme case in order to make the argument plain. It may be true there is some difficulty in obtaining a conviction for such an offence, but you cannot make that a justification for rendering a man liable to an offence that he is no more guilty of than the man in the moon. You have got to take care that your legislation is so worded that nobody who is really innocent shall be convicted. But you can convict the whole world under this wording. It needs revision.

The provision may be unnecessarily wide-I will be quite candid with my hon. friend-at the same time nobody is going out to pick up a person on Wellington street and because he did not do something find him guilty of an offence under this bill. We have to assume that a little modicum of common sense will be exercised in the administration of the law. Having regard to my right hon. friend's legal acumen and his analytical power to split hairs and dissect a piece of legislation, I would possibly take the same position as he does, and allowing for everything I think perhaps it is too wide and not sufficiently definite. Rather than take the necessary time to redraft section 8, we will let it stand.
Section stands.
On section 9-Entering premises; assisting
the inspector.

I think the minister will observe that this section really covers all that he needs. I have not been able to follow it carefully, but have not observed any previous difficulty about it. With section 9 as the minister desires to have it passed, he does not require the part of section 8 that I have objected to as being loose.
Section 8 deals with obstruction.

Yes, and here the section defines what obstruction is, and so widely that he does not need the provisions of section 8 at all. If the minister gets a real draftsman to go over the sections again, he can shorten it up by saying that anyone who is guilty of an obstruction shall be liable to such-andi-such a penalty, because he has defined obstruction in section 9.

I suggest that the word " employee " be struck out. I do not think it would be fair to have an officer apprehend an employee who is under the control of a master and say that he shall be exposed to a fine. The same idea would apply to section 8. Why should an inspector come in and say to an employee, " You do this ", or " you do that ", without the consent of the master? I do not think an employee should be subjected to that.
It might be a joint stock company or something of that kind, and it would be very difficult to get at them.

There is no doubt about what the minister wishes to cover, but the last clause will cover it all. The difficulty with the first clause is that it did not define who came under its provisions; it might apply to anyone. This says: "all manufacturers or dealers in dairy products and their employees and all common carriers, railway, steamship ''-and so on. That makes all the provisions that are required, in my judgment, and the other clause only requires a very slight change.

The first clause
deals with obstruction and the other does not.
It makes the clause so that it will apply to anyone.

No man can serve two masters, and the employee is under the order of his master and is paid by him, and the government inspector has no right to come in and say, " You do this or I will fine you ".

Dairy Industry Act

Quite a number of these creameries are joint stock companies with a large number of shareholders, and very likely none of the shareholders 5 p.m. will be there. The creamery is operated by the employees, and if you exclude the employees whom will you prosecute? I think the clause is all right as it stands.
You could say the manager and not the employee.

The manager and
all the employees.
Section 9 agreed to.
On section 10-Regulations. Subsection (1) -Definition, etc.
The term "or constituents thereof " means ingredients like salt and colouring.

The draftsman here has not followed his rule, and one has to go back to the act in order to get the slightest idea of what this means. I do not think it will do any good to read it; one has to study it. The effect of (a) is this: That in addition to empowering to make regulations as to classification, marking and branding of butter and cheese and other dairy products, parliament proposes to empower the Governor in Council to make new definitions of butter, cheese and other dairy products or constituents thereof. There might be need of more definition of the constituents, but there is certainly no more need of definition of the products. I do not know why the word " definition " is put in at all. So far as (a) is concerned I do not see what the amendment is for. We have everything defined in this act so widely that surely we do not need to give the Governor in Council power to define it again.
There are quite a number of things we have not defined.
The constituents, perhaps.

There are rennet,
salt and colouring matter, and these are all important, especially the salt.

No, I see. In order to get power to define the constituents the amendment must carry, and I do not object to giving the Governor in Council power to define the constituents, but as to giving power to define butter and cheese and other dairy products, surely they are all defined in the act now.
[Mr. A. E. Ross.}

Take this kraft
cheese.
Is that not defined?

It is not defined.
New dairy products are being constantly put on the market and unless we have fairly wide powers to cope with changing conditions by means of order in council I shall only have to come back to parliament frequently to secure amendments. I understand that kraft cheese was one of the things we had in mind. Three or four members of the agricultural committee were under the impression that we should make regulations controlling the export of that product. If this particular article increases I think we shall sooner or later be obliged to define it; at present no one knows what its composition is.

I think it is absolutely
necessary that the minister should be given a certain degree of latitude in the matter of regulations, particularly in view of the constantly changing conditions of the market. Very often articles are adulterated and put upon the market in competition with legitimate products and it is important that regulations should be made on short notice to meet such a situation.

What we are providing will meet the difficulty suggested by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart).
Subsection (1) agreed to.
On subsection (2)-Seizure and confiscation.

What is the change
here?

This merely adds
certain words to make the provision more comprehensive. By an omission the added words were not underlined.
Subsection (2) agreed to.
On subsection (3).
This is all new.

This provides regulations with regard to the construction of cheese boxes. We have had a great deal of complaint from our representatives on the other side of the Atlantic regarding the condition of cheese boxes on their arrival in the-Old Country. For many years our cheese boxes have been made of very flimsy material and although they are subject to the control of the railway commission it has happened in actual practice that by the time the boxes-have been landed in England they have become sadly dilapidated, so that one would.

Dairy Industry Act
think they had passed through a cyclone. I have received photographs of Canadian cheese boxes landed in England, with complementary pictures of Australian boxes, and the contrast was anything but flattering to us. There is no question that the proper container has something to do with the sale of an article even in such a practical market as the Old Country. There has been no uniformity in the matter of cheese boxes in this country; the thing has, so to speak, simply grown up, Topsy-like, during the past fifty years without any direction. The result is that we have had four different kinds of hoops for various grades of cheese, and boxes of four different sizes; and some manufacturers have actually turned out twelve varieties of cheese boxes. These containers have all been made out of more or less flimsy material and on the whole they 'have reflected great discredit on the business of this country. I think it is highly essential that there should be some uniform system to secure a better class of boxes. It is proposed to arrange for a standardized diameter both for the large boxes and for the small containers and to allow' shippers two or three years in which to utilize the boxes they have on hand and to enable the box-makers to dispose of the wood they have already sawn. This will avoid any loss in this direction. There will 'be no inconvenience to the shippers in changing the boxes. This matter has been discussed during the consideration of the estimates as well as in the agricultural committee, many hon. gentlemen who come from dairy districts agreeing that the provision is necessary. I have also consulted manufacturers and those generally interested in the business and they concur in the wisdom of the proposal, provided that they are allowed to use up the material they have at present on hand. Mr. Daoust, of the harbour board of Montreal, when he came back from the Old Country, called at my office and expressed surprise that an otherwise excellent product should 'be shipped in such an unsatisfactory manner.
Mr. Mac'LEAN (Prince):	Has any weight
been decided on in regard to cheese?

No, that will be
left to the factory. We are providing a standard diameter and the weight can be made up by the height of the cheese.

I understand that the delivery of our cheese in 'bad condition in the Old Country is due largely to the fact that the article does not fit the container and 232i
thus the box is frequently broken. Perhaps it would be well to have a standard weight of cheese. Butter is shipped in 56-pound boxes, so that there is a standard so far as that commodity .is concerned; but cheese ranges from 70 to 80 pounds.

If the cheese are
all of the same size there will be no trouble in fitting them into the containers.

Section agreed to.
On section 11, subsection (1)-Establishment of guilt for violation of act.

The words "prima facie
evidence" occur in this section. We have already amended one section in which similar words appear, and to make the present provision clearer I move that the words "prima facie evidence" be struck out and the words "prima facie proof" be substituted therefor.
Mr. MEI'GHE'N:	The minister will notice
that the draftsman did not follow his celebrated rule here.

I have no rule; I
do not pretend to be an authority on legal questions.
Are factories that manufacture butter and cheese required to register.
Yes.

Is there any penalty
provided for factories that are not registered using the registered number of some other factory?

Until a factory
secures a registered number we have authority to withhold our certificate for the butter or cheese which it turns out.

I think the amendment
is all right.
Amendment agreed to. Subsection (1) agreed to.

If the minister is anxious that the expense of the analysis should be actually included in the costs of the prosecution, he is not using the correct language, because the words, "shall be deemed," give the magistrate or judge discretion, in the matter.

I do not see any great
objection to giving the magistrate discretion. I can well imagine cases where the person accused should not pay the expenses of the analysis.
If he is convicted?
For instance, we refund fees in this House on certain bills.

I do not very often differ with the lhon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll), but I do not quite agree with him there. That is more concise, I admit, but I think it would have about the same effect.

It is not only shorter,

Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved that the House go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it ig expedient to provide,-
1.	That the Governor in Council may, from time to time, advance and pay to the corporation of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners, in addition to the moneys heretofore authorized to be advanced to the corporation for the construction of harbour improvements by existing legislation, such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of $5,000,000, as may be required to enable the corporation to complete construction of terminal facilities in Quebec harbour for which the plans, specifications and estimates have already been approved by the Governor in Council, and to construct such additional terminal facilities as may be, likewise, approved as necessary, further to properly equip the said port.
2.	That during the period of construction of the works referred to, the interest payable on the debentures to be deposited with the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, under the provisions of the proposed legislation, shall be deemed to be money acquired in the construction of such works and to be a part of the cost of the construction thereof, and may be paid out of the said sum of $5,000,000; the period of construction herein referred to shall begin on the day when the first advance is made on account of said construction, and terminate on such date as the Governor in Council shall determine.
3.	That no advances shall be paid, as above provided for, unless such detailed plans, specifications and estimates for the works on which the money to be advanced is to be expended as are satisfactory to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, have been submitted to and approved by the Governor in Council before work on the same has been commenced.
4.	That the corporation shall submit to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for approval, monthly applications for such advances as they may be entitled to apply for, with statements, in detail, in such form as the minister may direct, and, upon approval of same, authority for the payment of the amount applied tor may be granted by the Governor in Council.
5.	That the corporation shall, upon any advances being made, deposit with the Minister of Finance debentures of the corporation equal in par value to the advance so made, repayable wthin twenty-five years from the date of issue, and bearing interest payable half-yearly at the rate of five per centum per annum.

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
6.	That the principal and interest of the sums advanced under the authority of the proposed legislation to the corporation shall be payable by the corporation out of all its property, assets, tolls, rates, dues, penalties and other sources of revenue and income whatsoever, and shall rank as a charge thereon next after, and have precedence in regard to payment next after, the principal and interest of all debentures or bonds heretofore issued by the corporation to the public and amounting to the sum of one million one hundred and fifty thousand dollars, such debentures or bonds having been issued under the provision of chapter 48 of the statutes of 1898, chapter 34 of the statutes of 1899 and chapter 36 of the statutes of 1907.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of
the committee to consider this resolution section by section? Section 1.
I think, Mr. Chairman, that there should be a general discussion of the resolution before we consider it clause by clause.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The general discussion would be permissible on the first clause, which provides for the expenditure.

I think it would be
necessary to consider the last clause before we take up the first one. The last clause says:
The principal and interest. . . . shall rank as a charge thereon next after, and have precedence in regard to payment next after, the principal and interest of all debentures or bonds heretofore issued by the corporation to the public and amounting to the sum of $1,150,000.
Has the Quebec Harbour Commission ever made any payment of interest or principal in respect to the bonds issued, and if so, how much?

The resolution is a very
extended one and contains practically all the details that it is proposed to incorporate in the bill. It provides for a loan not exceeding $5,000,000 for new facilities at the port of Quebec. This request on the part of the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec and on the part of the citizens of Quebec has been made to the present government and was made also, I believe, to previous governments, but action has been delayed up to the present. I think we are now justified in granting the request, which has received the approval, I may say, of the companies interested in shipping. In these days of keen competition among trading countries it would seem to be the duty of governments to do all they can to provide necessary facilities at the ports of the country in order to facilitate the handling and transport of goods, which is one of the most interesting and most difficult problems we have to deal with. Canada is one of the most
important trading countries of the world; it is necessary that she should build up her ports and through that development lead to the development of the country as a whole. Expenditures which have already been made upon our ports have proved to be profitable to the public at large. The ports of Montreal, Vancouver, St. John and Halifax are a credit to the country; I think we are all proud that Canada has such facilities. It is by and through its ports that a country is best known abroad; it is through the traffic in and out of our ports that Canada becomes better known to all other countries with whom she has to deal. Montreal is to-day one of the most important ports of the world, and unquestionably its development has played a large part in the progress of all this part of the country. There is room for further development at Quebec also, located1, as it is, at the centre of a very interesting district. When our country starts anew in its progress; when they enjoy in this part of the country the development toward which they are working, I think the port of Quebec will need all the facilities that we are capable of granting them. The government are following a proper policy, it seems to me, in trying to bring about as much development as possible in this port of Quebec, which is one of the greatest natural ports in the world; and I am confident that the result will be to bring about greater progress and expansion. I think, therefore, there can be no serious objection to this expenditure. What the harbour commissioners have in view is the building of a wharf, and the erection of sheds thereon, and the carrying out of some dredging. The proposed wharf will be nearly four thousand feet long, and upon it will be erected sheds for the housing of goods for loading on and off the boats. The work will start about three hundred feet east of what is called the car ferry wharf on the St. Lawrence and go up toward the Quebec bridge. The developments which have so far been carried out at that port have been rather at the mouth of the St. Charles river, at the east side of the city. These proposed developments are to take place on the St. Lawrence in front of the city of Quebec. I said a moment ago that this project was approved by people interested in navigation. It will be well to place on the record the approval of this project which has been given by the Shipping Federation of Canada. This association has sent to the Prime Minister an approval covering the project that the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec have in mind.

What is the
date of that?

Quebec Harbour Commissioners

24th March, 1924. This
memorial reads:
The memorial of the Shipping Federation of Canada, incorporated by act of parliament of the Dominion of Canada, who own or represent 977,799 gross tons of ocean and coasting shipping trading to the St. Lawrence route, with a capital investment of many millions of dollars, a considerable portion of which is for Canadian account.
1.	Whereas the accommodation at the port of Quebec for the larger cdass of vessels is .entirely inadequate, and the draft of water available will not permit using ports above Quebec, and,
2.	Whereas, the berths available for ocean-going vessels at the port of Quebec are now all allotted for the coming season of navigation and accommodation is unavailable for any other vessels which may desire to trade to Quebec, and
3.	Whereas at the present time a large passenger liner company is seeking accommodation for its vessels at the port of Quebec and none is available, and
4.	Whereas fully two-thirds of passengers and cargo arriving at the port of Quebec is destined to other provinces in the Dominion, and
5.	Whereas the St. Lawrence route is the principal artery of the trade and commerce of the Dominion, and any trade diverted to ports to the south of us through failure to provide adequate accommodation would be a national loss, and
6.	Whereas the government have already spent large sums of money in improving our aids to navigation, and the increased trade which has resulted therefrom during the past twenty-years has fully compensated the country for the expenditures made, and
7.	Whereas the travelling public prefer to go direct to or from their homeland or their intended protracted sojourn without passing through foreign territory, and
8.	Whereas your memorialists have had submitted to them by the Quebec harbour commissioners a general plan providing for the present and future requirements of the port of Quebec, which has received the unanimous endorsement of your memorialists, and
9.	Whereas your memorialists feel reluctant in recommending this plan to the government at such a time of financial stringency, but, nevertheless, are strongly of the opinion that unless Canadian routes are developed to the fullest extent possible, there is danger of Canada losing trade to competing ports to the south of us, where immense sums of money are being expended annually in providing modern ocean terminal facilities.
Therefore your memorialists are of the opinion that an appropriation should be granted to the Quebec harbour commissioners to enable them to commence this national work, as it may be pointed out that the matter is urgent when it is considered that it will take five years before any of the additional berths can be provided for the use of ocean traffic. .
Furthermore, your memorialists have the greatest confidence in the present Board of Harbour Commissioners and feel that any money voted by the government will be judiciously spent in providing accommodation for the present and future needs of the port of Quebec. The whole most respectfully submitted.
Wlliam I. Gear,
Chairman. Thomas Robb,
Secretary.
Although this approval was given in the month of March, 1924, the shipping federation entertains the same view.
Conditions have . entirely changed, that is all.

The condition of the
country-

Has entirely
changed and my hon. friend knows that.

I contend that the shipping federation entertains the same view in regard to the project. In answer to the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell), I may say that the harbour commissioners have paid the interest on the bonds issued to the public to an amount of $1,150,000. The interest has always been paid by the commissioners.
Have they paid any interest to the government on advances made by the government?
No.

I am one of those who believe the harbour of Quebec should be developed; but there is a consideration that comes before further development of Quebec harbour, and that is that the present harbour facilities shall be used to its full capacity. In this respect, I feel that an injustice is being done, not only to the port of Quebec, but to the Transcontinental railway and to the ports of Halifax and St. John. When the Transcontinental railway was built, we were told that it was built for the express purpose of furnishing a short direct route to the eastern seaboard, a route with the best grades of any road in Canada, and this was done at an enormous expense to this country. Traffic, has not gone over that road in the volume it should. For instance, the port of Quebec is nearer to Winnipeg by rail than is the port of Montreal. I think I am well within the facts in stating that. Moreover, the port of St. John is nearer Winnipeg by rail, using the Transcontinental railway, than the port of Portland is to WTnnipeg via Montreal. This has been a sore point with us in the Maritime provinces-for, I was going to say generations; at least, ever since the Transcontinental was built. If the government will guarantee that traffic will go over the Transcontinental in the shape of grain, cattle and other products coming from the west to the east, and products that the west needs going westward, we shall have no hesitation in assisting the minister in developing the port of Quebec. But until this is done, I feel quite reluctant to support this resolution or a bill based upon it. If the traffic were put over the Transcontinental that it is capable of handling, if the traffic were put through the port of Quebec that it is capable of handling with its present

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
facilities, and then something further were needed, the minister would be well justified in coming to this parliament to get a further loan for the Quebec Harbour Commission. For instance, when the minister's estimates were up a few days ago, I for one took the view that at present the channel should be deepened as far as the harbour at Quebec for large ocean-going vessels and not on to Montreal; that the port of Quebec should be developed to accommodate those vessels; and that traffic should be brought over the Transcontinental to Quebec to furnish cargoes for those ocean-going vessels. I still hold those views.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: How can that be done if the port of Quebec is not enlarged?

That is my point exactly. The point is that Quebec has not been given the traffic it can handle at the present time. We have over-built our railways, we have over-developed our ports in some directions, and we have carried to a port in the United States a large quantity of traffic that should go through Canadian ports. This has been done because east-bound traffic from the west has largely centred at Montreal. Then when water navigation closes to Montreal in the fall, we have an immense stock of grain and other products that must go overseas. It is a long haul from Montreal to Halifax or St. John as compared with the haul to Portland. If more of this traffic were centred at Quebec,-there will be plenty of traffic for Montreal, too-then when navigation closed, this surplus tonnage stored in the elevators at Quebec would go east to the Maritime seaboard, would furnish traffic for our Transcontinental railway to those ports in the east and would, I think, help to reduce the deficit on the Canadian National Railways. But, as I said, just as long as the whole traffic is headed for Montreal, we in the Maritime provinces have no hope of developing our ports and of getting the traffic that we feel we are entitled to and that we were promised at the time of confederation.
I think, possibly, the government but faintly realizes the feeling in the Maritime provinces that they have lost out by going into confederation, largely due to the fact that the promises made when confederation was entered into have not been carried out. I am not blaming any particular government for this failure but this is the sore point-the perpetual withholding of the fulfilment of the terms of confederation. While possibly we have nothing in black and white that we can produce to prove the promises made I think that all
the arguments used at the time to induce the Maritime provinces to come into confederation have been violated; at 'least nearly everyone of them with the exception of the promise to construct the Intercolonial railway, and even in that respect I feel that the representatives of the Maritime provinces at that time were just a little bit too slack. I think possibly they should have had more in black and white instead of the verbal promise of the Dominion government to construct and operate the Intercolonial railway. Of course, for many years the railway was operated not as a commercial enterprise but as a connecting link between the two portions of Canada. It was operated on a freight rate that was not a paying rate -it never was supposed to be a paying rate. However, at the present time the Intercolonial is part of the National system and I do not know that we are going to cause disruption by demanding that the line be taken out of the Canadian National system. I for one am not. I do think, however, that the Maritime provinces should have more consideration than they are getting now in the way of railway freight rates. It seems to me that this proposal might very well stand over, and in the event of a general election it might become a very illuminating and legitimate subject for discussion. If it is held over the government can give it a prominent place in their election literature and in their election orations, and if the people of Canada as a whole believe that such expenditures are justified then I will raise no serious objection. But I certainly think that I should be lacking in my duty at this time if I did not raise my voice in protest against this premature expenditure; and unless convincing information is submitted I shall vote against its adoption.

This appears to me
to be about the most remarkable vote that has come before parliament in the four years I have been in this House. The port of Quebec already owes something like $21,000,000 on which, according to the statement given by the minister, no interest has been paid since 1887, and the accrued interest at present is over $8,000,000. Now, I do not think than any hon. gentleman in this House would object to this expenditure if the money were going to be properly used and if there were some reasonable hope of its being paid back. But it seems to me the height of absurdity for the government to be spending more money on the port of Quebec while at the same time this very government is actually preventing our western produce going through that port. . Every session since I have been in this House I have raised my voice against that condition of affairs. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) two sessions ago treated my plea so sympathetically that I was encouraged to hope that something would be done. I noticed that about that same time Sir Henry Thornton promised that the question of rates over the Transcontinental railway to the port of Quebec would be dis- . cussed by his board of management. But nothing has come of it. Two years have gone by since that time, and those discriminatory-no, I will say, those prohibitive rates over our own railway to the port of Quebec are still maintained. Now, this government has it in the hollow of its hand to develop that port, and if it were making any serious

I should like to submit a few figures in connection with grain and other rates to the port of Quebec. Armstrong is a point on the Transcontinental railway due north of Port Arthur and Fort William, and for purposes of comparison it may be taken as the equivalent of those two points. Armstrong is 959 miles from Quebec, and the present rate on wheat from there to Quebec is 20.7 cents per bushel. This would appear to be about double the prevailing wheat rate on the prairies, as is shown by the following comparison. From Edmonton to Port Arthur the distance is 1,305 miles, about one-third further than the distance from Armstrong to Quebec, but the rate on wheat is only 15.6 cents per bushel. That, I may say, is what we commonly call the Crowsnest rate-the prevailing prairie rate to the head of the lakes. It is not necessary to quote any further figures. I think the case is very clearly established that a serious discrimination exists against the use of the Transcontinental railway and the port of Quebec. To-day we look on the construction of the Transcontinental railway as a monumental blunder. Even our Liberal friends say so. I have not heard one single hon. gentleman in the Liberal party during the lifetime of this parliament defend the construction of that railway. Now, I am not clear in my own mind that it was a blunder. I am rather inclined to think that the men who designed and carried that project through had a vision a little beyond that of the hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches today, because it was designed for the purpose of giving the farmers of the west the shortest possible route to the sea. But if the construction of that railway was a blunder, then I say it is a crime not to use it at the present time, but to maintain on it a prohibitory rate, a rate that prevents us using what is one of the finest pieces of roadbed on the continent of America. This magnificent road remains idle, and the port of Quebec is not given an opportunity to develop in the way that it should.
I wish to make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that I am not pleading for the port of Quebec. I do not need to. There are many hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches to-day who are better qualified than I am to put forward the claims and merits of that port.

Surely the government has some means of dealing with this situation? It is not impossible of solution. The only time that any grain goes forward to the port of Quebec by the railway is after the ports at the head of the lakes are closed in winter time, and when that grain is so transported it means that the unfortunate farmer receives about ten cents a bushel less than he is entitled to. But this is only part of the story. The farmers' interests are seriously prejudiced throughout the whole season when the grain is being moved by water from the head of the lakes. For the shipping season of 1921 the average cost of transporting wheat from the head of the lakes to Montreal via Port Colborne was 12.60 cents per bushel.
All rail?

No, all water. In addition there is .60 cents for insurance, making a total of 13.20 cents per bushel; the average for 1922 was 13.72 cents, plus .60 cents for insurance, making a total of 14.32 cents. Now, let us analyse these figures a little further. Taking the Edmonton-Port Arthur rate as the basis, the Armstrong-Que-bec rate will be 11 cents a bushel. Now, had this eleven-cent rate been in effect during the season 1921, our grain could have been delivered by rail at the port of Quebec for two and a fifth cents less than it was delivered to Montreal by water; and in 1922 for three and 
a third cents less. Taking the total amount of grain shipped from the head of the lakes during 1921 and 1922, an eleven cent rate would have saved the farmers of western Canada $7,273,000 in 1921 and $8,621,000 in 1922. To be fair, I should point out that in 1923 and 1924 the average water rate was less than the eleven cent rate. In 1923 the average cost of transporting our grain over the water from the head of the lakes to Montreal was 10.91 cents. In 1924 it was 8.99 cents, but there were certain periods in both those years when the rate went considerably above the 11 cent mark. For instance, in May, 1923, the average rate was 12.10 and in October. 12.61, and for the month of April, 1924, the average rate was 11.71 cents. In the figures I have quoted I am including only the grain actually shipped by water from the head of the lakes. I have not taken into account the grain that was ground in Canadian mills and went out as flour, neither am I considering the grain that went forward all rail to Quebec, much of which no doubt paid the double rate. Quebec is 150 miles farther down the river than Montreal.
One hundred and eighty.

I am glad to have my hon. friend's correction; that makes my argument all the stronger. Most of the insurance risk between Montreal and Liverpool is based on the risk in the St. Lawrence river, and this is almost, if not entirely, overcome when Quebec is reached; and that again is ano'.her factor. So in addition to saving the amounts I have already quoted, there is the advantage of being 180 miles nearer the market and the very much reduced insurance rate. Of course, I do not assume for a moment that if this low rate were put into effect all our grain would go forward all rail to Quebec; nobody would take that suggestion very seriously. But I think the assertion will not be challenged that if the 11 cent rate were in effect to the port of Quebec it would immediately create a maximum rate on the lakes, a rate that would be more effective in curbing the predatory instincts of the shipping combine than any legislation this House has passed or ever can pass. Now, this government made a rather feeble attempt some years ago to deal with the shipping combine on the lakes. I pointed out on that occasion, and I have pointed out repeatedly since, that the government had in the hollow of its hand the very means of dealing effectively with the combine, because just as soon as the rate was set at 11 cents a bushel we know that the lake rates would never go beyond that figure.

The question of the cost at which gram can be handled comes in, and I think it is an incontestable fact that both our railways have made very substantial profits in carrying grain at the rates in effect on the prairies, or from the prairies to the head of the lakes, since July 6, 1922. A careful analysis of railway statistics will convince anyone of that. If we just look at the lower earnings, the reduced profits of the railways this year, we will see that it is due very largely if not entirely to the fact that we had only half a crop of grain in western Canada. But if the question should arise at all as to the profitable nature of the business of carrying grain from Armstrong to Quebec at 11 cents a bushel. 1 would like to quote some figures that I think will supply the last connecting link in that chain of proof. I have some figures here showing the tonnage out of the various divisional points between Winnipeg and Port Arthur over the old Canadian Northern main line, and also between Winnipeg and Quebec over the National Transcontinental. I find on looking up these figures-and they are based on what is known as a 53 per cent engine-that the average tonnage from Winnipeg to Port Arthur via the old main line is 2,600 tons while the average from Winnipeg to Quebec over the Transcontinental is 3.205 tons, or 23 per cent more. That means that at the same cost per mile 23 per cent more grain can be delivered at Quebec than can be delivered at Port Arthur, so that the question of cost is all in favour of Quebec as against Port Arthur. There is no doubt that some of this grain came back to Montreal from Buffalo, but unquestionably the great bulk of it found its way to the ocean and thence to Liverpool through American channels, resulting in a loss of millions of dollars of earnings to our National railways, millions of dollars in wages to our working people, millions of revenue to our ports, and as well a deterioration in the value of our grain through its being mixed in transit. Incidentally I may say that one of our grievances in the west has been that the grain which goes out through American ports is contaminated in transit. While it is given a grading certificate at the head of the lakes, and when it goes to Buffalo that grading certificate follows it to Liverpool, very often it is an entirely different grade when it gets there. That has an effect in setting the price for the grades that are bought back on the prairies, and as such is one of the farmers' grievances. I would not have hon. gentlemen from the Maritime ports think for one moment that the farmers in the west are not interested in diverting this grain through our own ports and having it sent to Europe by that rou'.e instead of the American route.
To deal a little further with figures, I may say that the Canadian Pacific rate from Goderich to Halifax, 1,305 miles, is 121 cents a bushel, considerably less than the prevailing prairie rate, or the rate from the prairies to the head of the lakes. The rate from Fort William to Halifax, a distance of 1,753 miles, is 21.3 cents a bushel, while the rate from Armstrong to Quebec, only 959 miles, is maintained at 20.7 cents a bushel. I may say, Sir, that we in the west are interested in this question for another reason. It is generally admitted that no large cattle trade can be built up with Europe under prevailing conditions. In 1923 the United Grain Growers made a trial shipment of 600 steers from Winnipeg to Liverpool, and they shipped those steers over the Transcontinental to Quebec. Perhaps it is almost unnecessary to recount the circumstances connected with that shipment. A large number of members of this House went to Quebec to see the cattle loaded, and I think all those members were impressed with the superior facilities provided at that port for handling cattle. We found that whereas at Montreal the cattle were unloaded miles from the dock, and when ready for the vessel had to be loaded again and shipped from the railway to the vessel, at Quebec they were unloaded directly at the dock and when ready for the ship were driven on board without any further handling. Any cattle man knows that all this extra handling and unloading is very detrimental to the cattle; it means a considerable extra shrinkage. We were told by one of the men in charge of these cattle that taking all these factors into consideration-and I may say that the running time of the train between Winnipeg and Quebec was eighteen hours less than a train could have made to Montreal-taking all these factors into consideration, he said, the probable saving per head would be not less than $5 in favour of Quebec as against shipping these cattle to Montreal. I have a letter here from the first vice-president of the United Grain Growers in answer to a letter I wrote to him asking for some facts in connection with this

When we realize that the port of Quebec is 500 miles nearer to Liverpool than the port of New York, the question .arises: Why is it that this prohibitive rate is maintained? The government tries to wash its hands of the responsibility. Of course we know that no government can do so. Whose fault is
it that the freight is not routed over that northern route?
The fault is this government's, coupled with the management of the National Railways for maintaining a prohibitory rate.
Has the shipper not something to do with the routing of his stuff?

The shipper has a good
deal to do with it; but if my hon. friend were shipping a carload of wheat from Winnipeg, and he found that he could route it through the United States ten cents a bushel cheaper, he would not be likely to patronize the port of Quebec, and no other hon. gentleman would. This year all the sailings
of cattle on the Canadian Government Merchant Marine for the months of May, June and July, are booked for the port of Quebec,

and recently a shipload of cattle arrived over the Transcontinental and was shipped from Quebec. I do not know how many head there were.

below deck with grain?

No. I am simply giving
