Quebec for cattle, that means that they are going there considerably hampered and that the trade is being ruined in a way.
I agree with my hon. friend.

If we can make up
mixed cargoes at Quebec and those vessels do not have to go to Montreal for cargo, that means a difference of $5 a head. That would make a very considerable saving to the farmers of the west, and that is the only way in which we can ever secure the market in the Old Country. We are talking about developing the cattle trade. It costs to-day over $40 to deliver a steer from Winnipeg to Liverpool, and about $45, I believe, from Calgary. Any farmer knows it is impossible to develop - trade under those conditions. The difference of that $5 alone would mean that we might be able to build up a reasonably profitable trade.
Just why are these rates continued? Naturally when we see a discriminatory rate of that kind existing, we look around for a reason. I do not believe for one moment it is simply indifference or, as the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) would indicate, that the government finds that it has not the power. There is something wrong there. It is ordinarily said that this is due to the influence of the port of Montreal; that Montreal is jealous of developing a rival and is determined that Quebec will not be

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
developed any more than the Hudson Bay route. I do not accept that altogether. Surely it is not advantageous to the port of Montreal to be sending hundreds of millions of bushels of our grain through American ports. If the port of Quebec would handle only one-half of the grain that is taken through American channels to-day, that would not hurt Montreal at all. But I think the crux of the situation is the rate. Lake shippers are concerned not so much about the volume of trade as about the profitable rate it pays. They would1 rather have a small trade at a large profit, than a large trade at a small profit. They are not particularly w'orried about discrimination against our ports. They are not concerned whether Montreal or Quebec or any other port develops. They are concerned with one thing only, and that is the amount of dividends they can pay. As long as they have a rate that is not settled by anything, as long as there is no maximum rate, as long as whenever there is a period of congestion they can raise those rates and tax us eight or ten million dollars extra, as they did in 1922 and in 1921, they are not concerned with handling a large volume of trade. That, it seems to me, is the crux of the situation. It is hardly believable that this government, that the management of the Canadian National Railways would be so much under the influence of the shipping combine as that. I can scarcely credit that. I have a little more confidence in our political institutions than to accept such a suggestion. Therefore, there is a responsibility on this government. It must be in a position either to defend or to condemn this rate. I have discussed this for the last four years with every railway official I have met, men who know what proper rates are, men who have studied this situation for years, and I have yet to run across a single railway official who will defend this rate. This government does not defend it. There is not a minister of the crown to-day who will say that it is necessary to maintain this rate. There is not an hon. gentleman on the Liberal benches who will say that. Sir Henry Thornton will not defend and has never defended this rate. In his answers to the Quebec Board of Trade, he gave them to understand that he was very sympathetic to a reduction of the rate, but his hands seemed to be tied. There is something in the way of giving us a reduction in the rate.
In conclusion, let me repeat what the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell) said. I am prepared to support this
project, if the government will give us an assurance that they are going to permit trade to come forward to develop the port of Quebec. Further, I think I can say that every hon. gentleman in this section of the House will support this resolution if the government will give us some assurance that they are going to remove this discrimination against their own railway and the port of Quebec. But if they fail to give us that assurance, I for one must vote against it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Why does
the railway board permit an excessive rate? The hon. gentleman says that it is a discriminatory rate on that particular line. Rates are not a matter for the government.
I do not think that is a proper question to come from the government. That is something the government should answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon.
member says that the government must interfere with the rate. The government will not interfere with the rate. That is a matter for the railway board. If there is a discriminatory rate, the railway board is very precise in dealing with it unless it is a statutory rate.

It certainly is a discriminatory rate. If the Minister of the Interior will look into the figures, I think he will admit and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will admit that it is discriminatory. This matter has been discussed by the railway board, and I have no doubt the government knows just what the railway board thinks about it. I cannot believe the railway board at a meeting discussed this matter without the government having some knowledge of it. The government has the responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Only in
case of appeal.
In any case, the government has this responsibility right now, that it should refuse to vote a dollar more for development work at Quebec untii that port has some opportunity of getting traffic.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
really think my hon friend can argue that only the traffic that comes over the Transcontinental comes to the port of Quebec. Because that is the only port at which the bigger ships coming up the St. Lawrence can
3646	COMMONS
Quebec Harbour Commissioners
berth to-day. It must get some traffic; all the business coming up the St. Lawrence does not go to Montreal. I am not denying, of course, that if more traffic went over the Transcontinental it would not help the situation.

I am quite aware that we get a good traffic at the port of Quebec. But I think the minister must admit- particularly in view of the fact that we spend millions and millions every year to enable larger ships to go to Montreal-that we are doing something annually to take away trade from Quebec. Sometimes I think it was a mistake to ever develop the port of Montreal; that is my humble opinion. I think grain can be moved more cheaply to Quebec by railway to-day than it can be moved through the circuitous route over the lakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
'Vith much that my
hon. friend has said I would not like to disagree. Indeed, he has used figures and arguments that I was going to use and I shall not repeat them. I think he and I might reach a common ground of understanding if he only uses a little good will. Personally I am willing to contribute my share of that good will. It is true, as my hon. friend said that when the Transcontinental railway was built the people of Canada were not only given to understand but were told that it would be used for the carrying of products from the west to the Atlantic ports, especially grain; that the distance by this route would be considerably shorter; that the grades would be much lighter, as they are; and that facilities would be provided at the ocean ports to handle all the traffic that offered. Indeed, pieces of land have been purchased on the waterfront of the St. Lawrence river from Quebec to Sillery by successive governments. This land was thus acquired by the country for that very purpose. However, I am free .to admit that the promise made at the time has not been carried out to the extent it should have been.

To what ex'ent has the
promise been made good.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, the road has been built but it has not been used in the way it should have been. I am quite willing to say that I agree with my hon. friend when he says the rate is much too high on the Transcontinental as far as the port of Quebec is concerned. Our western friends have always complained about it. In 1920 twenty-two senators and members of parliament representing the west wrote a letter to the then Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden,

dated Ottawa, 26th September, relating these facts, complaining that the rates were made so high as lo prohibit the use of the Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg or Armstrong to Quebec- and asking that sufficient additional grain storage be built at Quebec, Halifax and St. John to handle the business of Canadian grain "which we believe it would be possible to win back from New York if these suggestions are adopted." This communication was signed by the representatives of the west both in the House of Commons and in the Senate in 1920. In 1921, my hon. friend will see, steps were taken to try to redress what appeared to be a grievance. In that year the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec made representations to the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada complaining about this rate, and an investigation was held by the 'board, presided over by the late Mr. Carvell, in Quebec city. I have here the evidence that was given at that time and the arguments advanced, and I find the extraordinary argument used by the then chief commissioner that apparently if the rates were reduced as conditions would justify their reduction it would mean ruin for the other railways and that this could not be done. I quote from the statement of the chief commissioner as reported at page 2755 of the record:
I can hardly agree with that. If my conception of the National Transcontinental was right when it was started and when it was being built I think freight can be transported over that line at a figure which would mean the absolute ruination of other railways in Canada. If not we were all wrong and we were not justified in building it.
And then Mr. Commissioner Rutherford, as reported at 2756 says:
This is something that has to be general in a very careful way. When we, consider the elevator systems at Fort William and Port Arthur, the tremendous machinery created for the movement of that grain crop to introduce a revolutionary method like the making of a speoial rate on any one road would mean disturbing the whole movement of grain, such a disturbance as would bring about economic disaster for the time being.
The whole purport of the discussion between the representatives of the harbour commission and the board of trade and the commissioners was to that effect. It was practically admitted that the rate was too high, but to reduce it would have meant, according to some of the arguments presented, disaster for-the other roads.

Just before the minister leaves that point would he permit a question? Have the people of the city of Quebec ever appealed at any time to the Governor in Council against the discrimination?

Quebec Harbour Commissioners

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think there
was an appeal from the ruling of the board at that time.
Has there ever been an appeal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think so. I
speak subject to correction but I think there was no appeal from the ruling.

There was an appeal to the government and there have been unofficial appeals. In 1920 a memorial was presented to the Privy Council at Ottawa by the mayor of Quebec, who was accompanied by a deputation of citizens. That memorial has been printed.
When was that, in 1920?

On January 19, 1921. In
that memorial the whole question of rates and of the harbour was discussed; it is a formal appeal.
Was that a formal appeal from the decision of the railway commission?
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, it was not. This
was followed in 1922 by an investigation in the other chamber of this parliament. The late Senator Bennett took a prominent part in that investigation, and the report of the committee of the senate, which was adopted by the upper chamber, concludes as follows:
That the government be advised:
(1)	To cause rates to be granted upon export grain over the Canadian National railways to Quebec, Montreal, Halifax, St. John and Vancouver such as would develop trade to the above ports.
(2)	As a corollary to the recommendation in paragraph one, that necessary elevator accommodation should be provided by the Dominion at Canadian ports.
(3)	To arrange with the marine underwriters or others in such a way that the marine insurance rates from Canadian seaports be as cheap as from the United States seaports.
So that the Senate also has found that the rates there were too high and recommended that steps be taken to have them reduced.
Judging by their recommendation, I think the Senate hold the same opinion as I hold, that the government had some responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that the
whole question of freight rates on railways is going to be discussed in this House, and I think that when the question comes up it will be the proper time to discuss it. My hon. friend would not ask me to give an opinion just now, but I may say that I agree 233
with him that the rate to Quebec is too high, and if I can do something to reduce it,-if this has any effect on the decision of my hon. friend-I will tell him that I am going to try to help them to reduce it.

May I be
permitted to suggest to the minister that if that is his argument it would be advisable for him to withdraw this resolution until after the freight rates have been decided.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend is logical in that position, when he knows that it would take five'years to build the work which it is proposed to build with the money asked for by this resolution I do not think it would be advisable to wait until there is a dhange in the freight rates to do it.
Does the minister suggest that it will take five years to get the rates down to the proper level?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. I hope it will
be possible to do that in a day or in a few days, but it will take five years to complete the necessary development in Quebec, and for that reason it is urgent and important that we should proceed now.
Apart altogether from this question of grain, and a larger proportion of wheat and cattle being shipped to Quebec, there is the necessity for the development of the port, even for the traffic which is handled there now. I do not agree with my hon. friend when he says that there are already more than sufficient facilities at Quebec for the traffic. Every berth was rented and occupied during the last season of navigation. There is no space available for the new vessels, which would come to the port of Quebec.
If the accommodations are all used how is it they cannot even pay interest on the investment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am going to tell my
hon. friend why; it is especially because the bulk of the traffic at Quebec is passenger traffic. Last year 75,000 people landed in Quebec and they did not pay one
9 p.m. cent to the harbour commission. Every little box of goods which is carried to Montreal is paying a rate for the use of the wharf there, but all the people who travel to the other provinces of Canada, and -who use the port of Quebec in landing, do not pay one cent to the commission.

That bears out my
argument that we should provide rates which



Quebec Harbour Commissioners
would enable those goods to be shipped through Quebec, and make that port the terminus of the ocean voyage instead of Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I agree with my hon.
friend in that statement. I do not want him to believe that I am opposed to further use being made of the port of Quebec.

I do not suggest that
for one moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But the hon. gentleman
wants me to say why they have not paid interest. It is because the port of Quebec is a national port, used in the general interests of Canada, and especially for the passenger traffic, but it has not been a paying traffic. The harbour commissioners of Quebec have been applying to the government in many instances for their approval, and I believe they have enacted a by-law to remedy the difficulty, but the government has always refused to approve of such a by-law, because the steamship companies represented that it would hurt the St. Lawrence route and the traffic of these companies. The harbour commissioners of Quebec have passed by-law to impose a tax of one dollar on every immigrant and passenger using the port of Quebec when landing. It is done in other parts of the world. It is done in the continental ports of Europe where the traffic is especially a passenger traffic. I have seen that myself and read about it.

Is that done in other
Canadian ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it is.
St. John or Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is talking about St. John. The hon. member is usually fair but he made a remark this afternoon about the Quebec Harbor Commission not paying interest, and suggesting that it should be charged compound interest. How much has St. John paid to the government for works built there ?

I suggested that the
government should get the harbour commissioners to issue bonds to cover the unpaid interest, as they did in other cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Why not apply it to
St. John?
Surely.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The improvements have
been built there by the Public Works department, not charged to anybody and nobody is
LMr. Campbell.]
complaining about it. Millions of dollars have been spent there and the very gentlemen who have been favoured in this way are asking that Quebec should be made to pay interest every year on every dollar that has been spent at Quebec. In Halifax everything has been built, I understand, by the Department of Railways and Canals, as part of the expenditure of the Intercolonial Railway.

As far as the expenditure at St. John is concerned, I do not agree that it was all wise. I think there has been a development at St. John which is absolutely absurd and the expenditure upon which has been wasted. I refer to Courtenay bay. While money has been expended here, the place where we need the facilities has been starved.
I am not blaming this government particularly; it has been done by several other governments in the past. I think the time may come when we will need Courtenay bay, but it was premature to spend so much money there and starve that part of the harbour of St. John that is really in use, and which needs more facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not want to discuss the question whether the expenditure at St. John was necessary or not. It was a part of the system, and the same may be said of Halifax, where not very long ago about twenty million dollars was spent, which is a good deal more than all the advances which have been made to the harbour commissioners of Quebec. Nobody is complaining about them not paying anything to us, but the system has been introduced in that way. As far as the port of Quebec is concerned, the interest has been charged on works which were really national works in such a manner that it was absolutely impossible for the harbour commissioners of Quebec to make both ends meet and pay the interest on the advances which had been made. Let me instance one thing: The government of Canada-I do not mean this government particularly-has built a pier in the harbour of Quebec which has cost one million dollars. It was built by the Public Works department. The work has been transferred to the harbour commission, charged to the harbour commission as an advance or as a loan, interest being added every year on that million dollars, and for what purpose has this pier been used? Only for the purpose of the Immigration department of the Canadian government. The pier and the shed and the buildings there are used for no other purpose than the work of immigration; and we are

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
charged interest on the amount. We are not receiving one cent and we have been charged $1,000,000 on that pier, which as I say is entirely at the disposal of the Immigration department. I ask the committee, is that fair? Am I not right in the statement that this is a national port and should be so considered, and that we should not be constantly hearing about this amount of interest not having been paid on the investment of the government?

I was not particularly complaining of the failure to pay the interest. As a matter of fact I have a good deal of sympathy with the harbour commission and I think the present condition is due largely to the fact that the legitimate trade of the port is not properly developed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not complain that my hon. friend has not been fair in that respect; far from it. The hon. member has put up a plea for a greater use of the port of Quebec which I could not equal, and I agree with him in many of his statements. I only wish that his conclusion had been as sound as his premises in this matter. Let me assure hon. gentlemen opposite that the large vessels cannot go above Quebec; whatever may be done in the way of dredging or otherwise vessels of over 16,000 tons will not take a chance on going above Quebec.
And yet it is proposed to spend $16,000,000 in an endeavour to take them past Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend is not logical. He opposes, as he and his friends opposed the other day, any expenditure for the further dredging of the channel between Quebec and Montreal, on the ground that it would be a useless expenditure especially at this time; and they argue that the vessels should use the port of Quebec. If they were on sound ground in that regard1 at that time, are they logical to-day in opposing the necessary facilities for the use of the port of Quebec?
If the minister takes that position, both votes cannot be justified.
Which one would you rather have?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen are not reasonable there either. Montreal is at the mouth of the canal system; it is at the head of navigation in that part of the country. I am free to admit that the bulk of the traffic, the larger portion of it, will always go to Montreal as far as this is possible. If the 233i
vessels can use the channel between Quebec and Montreal they certainly will go on to Montreal because it is always more economical to go as far as possible by water route. But there is room for the use of both harbours. Hon. gentlemen have admitted this, in advocating that as much traffic as possible should go through Canadian rather than American ports. But surely Montreal is not able to handle all the traffic alone.
Does the minister think that the country at this time has money for both of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the country at the present time must equip its trade routes as other countries are doing. There are other countries that suffered in the world war to a greater extent than Canada did, and they are building their trade routes and equipping their ports. This being the case, I do not think that a young and growing country like Canada can afford to neglect the proper development of its ports to handle its exports, the increase in which every year is something which we in Canada are proud of.

May I remind the minister
that they are doing this and not attempting to pay their debts?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
wants to be fair, and I have already explained to him that it was impossible for the port to pay under the circumstances that have been stated. If when amounts are asked year after year for public works, on ocean and river, there is a demand for some return on the money spent, I do not think that much will be voted under such conditions.

The minister misunderstood
me; in the remark I made I was referring to nations that are developing their trade routes although they are not paying their debts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is of the utmost importance that our ports should be properly equipped for the handling of traffic. I regret any objection that may be raised against the development of the St. Lawrence route for the use of large vessels. I heard the statement made the other day that if large ships cannot go on the route we should have small ones. It seems to me that the tendency is to have all types of vessels in modem navigation: and the St. Lawrence route is one of the finest waterways in the world. We have so built it that much of the passenger traffic which formerly went through New

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
York is now going to Quebec and Montreal. It is necessary therefore that we should make it possible for all types of vessels to use the route. And it has been equipped for that purpose; it has a dry dock which is one of the largest in the world and in which all sorts of vessels can be repaired.
Is the cost of the dry dock included in the total indebtedness of the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No; it was built by the Department of Public Works.
What is the cost of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot say.

Has that dock ever
been used?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is used all the time. I cannot understand the lack of knowledge of some hon. gentlemen as to the conditions in the port of Quebec. That dry dock is used every week in summer if not every day, and it has been used by some of the largest vessels that go on the St. Lawrence route. It would be a pity if we had no such dry dock on the St. Lawrence. If hon. gentlemen think, as the hon. member seems to believe, that this dry dock has not been used, I can understand that they would1 be reluctant about voting for the present resolution. But I beseech the hon. member to make himself better acquainted with the facts. The dock, I repeat, is being used; and it is highly essential that it should be there. And when hon. gentlemen argue that the port of Quebec is the natural outlet for shipments to bring about a lowering of rates on the Transcontinental route, surely they will realize that this cannot be done, that the port cannot be used, if the necessary facilities for the handling of traffic are not provided.
The minister is well acquainted with the letter which Mr. Scott, a member of the Royal Grain Commission, wrote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Mr. Scott's whole plea, as
I understand it, was to have freight alone sent to the port of Quebec; he makes no plea for extra facilities. That is the feature of his argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is the main plea,
but my friend should read some of the letters I have from Mr. Scott, when 'he would see that that gentleman claims this resolution is necessary.
lMr. Lapointe.]

Mr. Scott may be pleading for that too, but in the circular letter sent the members of the House he has not featured that part of it, and I think the minister who has charge of the resolution (Mr. Cardin) admits that extra facilities are not particularly necessary at the present time, that indeed the facilities now there are not being used. I recollect being at Quebec two or three years ago, and the harbour commissioners told me that they had facilities there sufficient to handle five times as much grain as was being offered.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Surely, I agree with
that.

If it is a question of charging immigrants, give the board license to do so, but use the facilities now there before asking this impoverished and groaning country to assume this further obligation. I want to remind the minister and the governm uit again, as I did the other night, that we have a vast hinterland that is providing one and three quarter million dollars of federal taxation every year for the building of these harbours and ports, and the people there are groaning under the burden of taxation. We are simply pressing the objections of our people back home in opposing these extra expenditures.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My friend will understand that grain, important as it is-and I agree with him on that-is not the only thing, and if he asks my friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin), for certainly he has not understood the minister correctly, he will be told that although ail the facilities are not being used there for the shipping of grain, they are being used for other purposes.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister
of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) a few moments ago lamented our ignorance about conditions at Quebec. I do not think any group in this House has taken more trouble to travel over the country and find out local conditions for themselves than have my friends around me. We have been willing to do that at all times. If my friends from the province of Quebec can tell us that they have taken as much interest in the west, for instance, and seen for themselves the conditions there as my friends around me have taken to become personally acquainted with conditions in the province of Quebec and the Maritime provinces, I should like to hear it.

Quebec Harbour Commissioners

We do not have to travel;
we take everything said by my hon. friends as gospel.

Is the hon. member
ready to take what we are saying now as gospel?

I am glad to hear my hon.
friend is converted, but it is only lately. When we went to Quebec we were very sympathetic towards their problems. I remember telling my friends when I was speaking to them there that the future of Quebec was tied up with the National Railways.
Mr. MEIG-HEN:	The National Policy.

No, the National Railways.
When the minister talks of cattle going down to Quebec this year, I should like to know whether those cattle are paying the same rate from Quebec as from Montreal, Quebec being the shorter route by 214 miles. The minister seems to deplore our doubting whether all the facilities at Quebec are being used. I may say-and in this again I shall be supported by my friends around me-when we went to see the dry dock there we entered an immense workshop covering a city block in area, and there was half an inch of dust on every implement and only one or two men around the building. We were told that there had not been a ship in that dry dock. If my information was wrong, I cannot help it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What time of the year
was that?
I believe in June-Ma>\

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think it was in May.

Perhaps it was. But that
was the information we received, and we did not know any better. If it was wrong, I am glad to be corrected.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It was certainly wrong.

We found a big shed for the
receipt of merchandise turned into a cattle dock with a great big pen built all through it. We asked why this had been done, and were told that no merchandise was received at the port of Quebec, it was all being carried on to Montreal. Now, the difficulty I find myself in is to know what to vote for, whether to vote this money for the harbour of Quebec to be developed, or to vote 816,000,000 to carry goods past Quebec. Both proposals cannot be right, in my opinion. But if they are both right, Mr. Chairman, I want to
say that it is not a bit of use our talking economy either in this House or in the country and then making these expenditures. I find myself unable to support this proposal.

At this point may I ask
the minister a question? Does he think that Canada should continue deepening her waterways and her harbours and building huge canals to satisfy the obsession of the shipping companies in continuing to build greater and still greater ships, while the evidence adduced before (he Shipping committee is that these big ships are most uneconomical in operation, and that the smaller, slower ships are the cheaper to run? To me it would indicate that we are heading in the wrong direction.

Mr. Chairman, will the
minister advise me whether the ports of Vancouver and Quebec are national ports? Based on that I have another question to put to him.
Certainly they are.

Before dinner I asked the
minister for the total indebtedness of the port of Quebec, for the gross revenue and the net revenue earned by the harbour commission of Quebec' and for similar figures for the ports of Montreal and Vancouver. The minister stated that he would get those figures for me. Can he give them out now?

Mr. Chairman, I think
my hon. friend misunderstood me. I promised him that I would get these details when we were in committee on the bill, because I had not the figures before me at the times and the officers had left the department. But I have some figures, although they are not a complete answer to the question of my* hon. friend. The total expenditure on the harbour development in Montreal to December 31, 1924, was $39,732,992.52, and the total amount advanced to date to the Montreal Harbour Commission is $39,730,000.
At what rate of interest?'
At 3, 34 and 5 per cent.
Are those the same rates as are charged Quebec and Vancouver?
The rate charged Vancouver is 5 per cent.
Why the difference?

The 3 and 34 per cent
rates apply to old loans, when the rate of interest was much lower than it is now. Upon the relatively recent loans the rate is 5 per cent everywhere.
3652	COMMONS
Quebec Harbour Commissioners
What rate is charged Quebec?

Five per cent. At Montreal there is no interest unpaid. At Vancouver the total expenditure on works of harbour improvement and development to December 31, 1924, was 811,513,269. The total advance to date has been $10,34o,900, and interest unpaid, amounts to $225,291.49.
Does that mean that there is some unpaid bond interest which has had to be paid by the government, or is it old interest for some years gone by?
It is for interest owing at the present time.

I think some explanation of this might be given. Is it not the case that in respect to new works of construction in respect to which no revenue is earned, the interest accumulates as construction goes on?

I am informed that the
country owes the harbour commission, at Vancouver, a certain amount for work which they have done, and when this money has been paid, the commission will be in a position to pay the interest.
In other words, it is held back as an offset against money owing by the country to Vancouver, so that there is no default either at Montreal or Vancouver in the payment of interest?
No.
Does the amount given as .expended on Quebec harbour include the money spent by the Department of Public 'Works? If not, how much has been spent on the harbour by the Department of Public Works?
I have not the exact information at hand, but I am inclined to think that the amount expended by the Public Works department is not included in this.
The minister has no information as to the amount that has been spent by the Public Works department?
I am afraid I have not that information here.
Does the minister know that something like half a million dollars was voted for Quebec harbour last year through the Public Works department?
Yes.
It is probable that a considerable amount has been spent by that department.

There was a vote last year of $500,000 in the Public Works department - for the harbour of Quebec. With the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the Minister of Justice I visited the harbour of Quebec and it was thought better that that vote should be administered through the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Accordingly it was transferred to that department, and as I understand it the expenditure has been made under the harbour commission.
How much df that was spent?
I have not that information, but I can get it for my hon. friend.
What new facilities are requiied at the port of Quebec?

I mentioned this afternoon what the expenditure was to be for. It is for the building of a wharf about 4,000 feet long, starting about 300 feet from the car ferry wharf; for the necessary dredging to provide a depth of 40 feet there, and for the building of sheds and the extension of railway trackage on the wharf.

How much is this wharf
expected to cost? Would the minister tell us also what are the present facilities at Quebec? What works have been provided with the money that has been voted in the past?

The facilities available at
Quebec include the following: steamship berths: in wet dock, six berths of from 400 to 500 feet in length; in tidal harbour, four berths or from 400 to 500 feet in length; breakwater, four berths of 500 feet in length, or three berths of 700 feet in length, or two berths of 1,100 feet in length; Pointe-a-Carcy wharves, four berths

one ocean, two coasting and one bunkering; river St. Charles basin, seven berths of from 500 to 600 feet in length. There is a grain elevator with a capacity of 2,000,000 bushels, with marine tower, conveyors and grain galleries. Its loading capacity is
60,000	bushels per hour. It has also a grain dryer, a Richardson separator, and a bagging shed. I know we can never provide facilities that will satisfy all the harbour commissioners, because we shall run out of money before we arrive at that happy position. I should like to quote briefly to show what some people in Quebec thought a few years ago they ought to have. In 1922 an hon. member from Quebec said:
We have got a grain elevator, but it is only a small one and not of the capacity we should have in the city of Quebec. An elevator of the proper capacity in that city would be a benefit to the country as a whole. Our elevator has a capacity of 2,000,000 or 3,000,000 bushels.
Sir Henry Drayton: A capacity of 2,000,000 bushels.
Mr. Lavigueur: We should have an elevator with a capacity of at least 10,000,000 bushels. That is what we were promised.
The elevator that is there handled last year a little over 4,000.000 bushels. I should like to know what we would have done with an elevator of a capacity of 10,000,000 bushels, and how much more the Quebec harbour commissioners would be in arrears of interest if we gave hon. members from Quebec what they really thought they should have. From the information which I have been able to gather from the minister, I am unable to see that Quebec is very badly in need of this additional S5.000.000 for work in the harbour. As I said before, I have no doubt they would like to have a great deal more money spent and more facilities provided. We would like to have more facilities sometimes in other parts of the country. In the section from which I come we would like to have had, two years ago, some more railway cars. There were not enough cars to move the crop away. Some farmers had to build bins to hold their grain, and some who could not afford to buy lumber threshed the grain on the ground simply because they could not get cars to take it away.

Does my hon. friend think
his section is the only one that suffers from shortage of cars?

No. But when we complained, we were told that the railway could not possibly be expected to furnish us right away with all the cars we needed and that we should be content to wait a while. I think there was some reason in that, and I think the same answer should be given to the Quebec harbour commission; that we cannot afford just now to spend $5,000,000 on this harbour; but that when they show more business through the port of Quebec and when this country can afford it, we should vote the $5,000,000 or whatever is necessary. I do not think any justification has been shown for .the vote. The speech that was made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) tonight sounds very much like the one which he made three years ago when $5,000,000 was granted to the harbour commission. They have come back and they seem to need the money quite as much as they did that $5,000,000.

Were it evident that
a large quantity of business was going through Quebec and that the export business was increasing, I think there would not be so much objection made apparent to this vote as there is. If it appears that a port is not being used to its full capacity and that a large volume of business is not being done through that port, it seems natural that an objection should be raised to the vote, and I quite see the force of it. W'e must, however, remember that the Transcontinental was built for various reasons, but that one important outstanding reason was that there should be direct transportation from Winnipeg and the west to Quebec for purposes of transhipment, and that most important of all this transportation was the question of grain. That expensive project was constructed largely for that purpose. We know now it has not been carried out. I think it should be carried out but it has not been. That, I think, is one of the reasons why objection was taken to the vote. It seems to me that Quebec has sound advantages, geographical and otherwise, such as should entitle it to a much larger volume of business than it is now receiving. It seems to me that the port of Quebec is particularly well suited for the transhipment of grain from Winnipeg and the west. Now, I would suggest to the government that they exert some pressure in this matter; it would be perfectly proper for them to do so. It is not a question of interfering with the management and operation of the Canadian National railways; the question involved is one of national policy for the country. When the government come and ask for this vote I think they should also be prepared to advise the Canadian National Railway board that the original idea contemplated by the construction of the Transcontinental railway should ibe carried out-that is to say there should be a substantial transportation of grain and other products from the west through the port of Quebec. I think the government have got this matter in their own hands. They should prove, what we believe should be established, that Quebec is capable of carrying on a large part of the export business of this country. I believe that if that fact were made evident-if it were made evident that the facilities which the government are asking for can be used and are going to be used; if there is substantial evidence of the

port being employed in the way originally proposed and in the manner which I think Quebec merits, I believe a large section of this country are willing that Quebec should be properly equipped, because such a proposal would not only be fair to Quebec but would help to solve the transportation problem of this country.
It does seem to me that under the circumstances the government would be well advised to allow the committee to rise and report progress, and consider this matter later on in the session-
No, no.

-after the freight rate question has received some consideration. We would then be in a better position to decide this question than we are to-night. I would very seriously submit to the government the propriety of so doing. I should like also to remark that personally I would have less reluctance to support this and other similar votes of money if we collected our revenue from the people of Canada in a different way. By the method we are following at the present time we are taxing industry and penalizing thrift and enterprise, and under those circumstances I have very little satisfaction in supporting any vote of money for what is, perhaps, in itself a very useful thing. I do not care to develop that idea any further at the present moment, but I do think the members of the House should seriously consider the relationship of expenditures to our methods of collecting taxation-the incidence of taxation. If we were to impose a different system of taxation it might not, perhaps, be a hardship upon this country to vote this amount of money and other large sums for similar development purposes. I may remark also incidentally that it seems very unfortunate that we should be confused as to the expenditure of money for this kind of work, sometimes through loans to harbour commissioners, sometimes through the Department of Public Works, sometimes through the Department of Marine and Fisheries; sometimes through the Department of Railways and Canals, and so on. We have asked to-night for information as to what amount has been spent in the port of Quebec under the Department. of Public Works, and what amount of that has been charged up to the harbour commissioners. We have not got that information. There seems to be a good deal of confusion on the subject, and I think it would be certainly very informative to the committee if,.

I desire to point out that this proposal is in the initial stage. It is a preliminary resolution that is being discussed. If this resolution passes will not the House be committed to the granting of this vote?

No, the House is never committed at any stage with regard to any matter by the passing of a resolution. The bill founded upon this resolution has to be introduced and after it receives its second reading the House goes into committee on the bill, and the whole matter can be dealt with without any commitments one way or the other.
Does not the passing of the resolution indicate that the House is favourable to the proposition?

If the
majority of the House wants to defeat a bill at any stage it can do so.

In taking that attitude the Minister of National Defence is resorting to strategy. The same attitude has been taken with regard to other measures brought in during the last five or six years and to my recollection the second reading of a bill has never been defeated after the resolution upon which the measure was based had been adopted.
Possibly owing to the lack of perseverance on the part of its opponents.

That may be, but it only goes to establish that the adoption of such an attitude by the minister is a piece of strategy, but it will not prevail in this case. I wish again to refer to certain statements in
a letter written by Mr. Scott, being reminded of the necessity for doing so by the statement of the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) when he alleged that there was discrimination against the port of Quebec in not providing sufficient traffic for the Transcontinental railway. It seems to me, according to the statements contained1 in the letter in question, that in the year 1904 when the Transcontinental railway was undertaken the railway company made an agreement with the Canadian parliament to provide all the shipping tonnage for the ports of Quebec and Montreal that would be necessary to accommodate the freight the railways might bring to those ports. When the government took over that line, according to the letter in question, it assumed all the obligations that the railway company had entered into. Consequently the failure to deliver the requisite amount of traffic to the port of Quebec is directly chargeable to this government. Let me point out this further fact: Only a few days ago hon. members from this comer of the House pleaded with the government to revalue the land of the soldier settler but the government were not responsive to the demands of the men who fought overseas; they declared that times were too hard to carry out such a policy. This lack of response of the government will be a dire disappointment to the soldier settlers. I do not think that the principle of soldier settlement was looked upon by parliament when it was adopted as an investment, but rather as a means of bringing peace and contentment to the country. Now the government are regarding the policy from an investment point of view, and they are asking the soldier settlers to repay in dollars and cents, by the expenditure of blood and sweat, moneys which were voted by this House for the purpose of pacifying the people. The government to-night is asking five million dollars to provide facilities in a harbour which already possess more facilities than are being used. Under the present condition, with our huge national debt, with no facilities afforded the people in the western country, we are asked to vote this large sum to the Quebec Harbour Commission. We know that when we have made a request for the construction of some small branch lines of railway we are told that there is no money available. Many electoral districts in this country are getting along without even a brick or a\stone.

I have six starving men driving on mail routes throughout my district, men working for fifty per cent of the money they earn; and yet I am asked to take the money raised by a federal tax paid by my people and spend it on this Quebec harbour.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Because it seems to me his remarks are beside the question.

I >am drawing my conclusions, and when hon. gentlemen interrupt me and speak about these branch railways, I am answering; it was not my suggestion. I just simply replied to them. The proposition is that the revenues that are taken from the hinterlands are to be put into sink holes of harbours which we do not require at the present time. When I listened to the recommendation of the Quebec harbour commissioners which the minister read I was persuaded that they had to go far afield to try and find reasons why we should vote this money. I am utterly and diametrically opposed to the expenditure of this money in the Quebec harbour at this time.

It gives me no pleasure *-and I will admit it-to assume any adverse attitude towards this vote. I have visited the city of Quebec I think three times. They have treated me very well and I like the city and the people; but I feel that I would be derelict in my duty if I allowed myself to be influenced by sentiment in something which must be a matter of business. If it were merely a question of sentiment, merely a desire to please or to help people whom I like, I would be delighted to do what I could. But I want to look at the question in a business way. As time has passed and I have become more acquainted with
10 p.m. the country as a whole, travelling through it and getting to know it better, seeing the results of public expenditure during the past twenty or thirty years, and considering the condition of indebtedness in which we find ourselves and the constantly increasing burden -fff 'taxation,-because in spite of some reductions at times the burden is increasing and* must increase as long as capital indebtedness increases-I have made up my mind ;imat I would vote for no large capital expenditures unless one of two con-
ditions was present, but if one of these conditions were present I would vote for it. In the first place I would vote for a large expenditure of public money by way of loan if it were a loan pure and simple; that is if the money were invested in such a way that the principle and interest would be returned to the government. I do not look upon that as an indebtdness but as an investment. Now is this condition present here? I hardly think that the history of the past would warrant such a conclusion. I am offering no criticism to the harbour commissioners of Quebec on account of the fact that they have not. made the interest payment. I realize the situation there, the nature of the investment and the impossibility of making .payment of either sinking fund or interest; but the fact remains that, in the light of the past financial history of the country, we cannot look upon this five millions as a direct addition to the national debt of the country, upon which they must pay annual interest. The other condition is this: if growing conditions and the demands of business imperatively called for such an expenditure, so that it was impossible to carry on the business of the country without it, and if the indirect benefit of the country through that expenditure would repay the country for that loan or that indebtedness, whether repaid directly or not, then I would support it. .
I would again frankly state that I have not been convinced1 either by what I have seen in Quebec-and I will admit that my personal knowledge and what I have heard to-night are superficial-that	under the present
business situation of the port and with the present tonnage offering the expenditure is warranted1 at this time. If, as has been suggested traffic conditions were such that we could reasonably expect a large and steady growth in the tonnage there, I would vote now for the expenditure; but as it is, as we have no such assurance, as we have simply to rest our case upon the experience of the past, I shall vote against it. When the time comes that the expenditure to my mind is warranted, when I see those conditions which I think are necessary to warrant the expenditure fulfilled, I shall be glad to support such a resolution if brought forward.

I cannot say how deeply
I regret the fact that we are not enjoying the support of some of the hon. members whom I especially esteem in this House, and who represent part of the country which, in my humble estimation is going to profit in the future more than any other part from the development of the facilities in the port of

Quebec Harbour Commissioners
Quebec. I say that in all sincerity because I am convinced that, though up to the present time an actual lack of facilities has not been evident in the port of Quebec, the time has come when our attention is called to the fact that in many respects the present facilities are taxed to their capacity. It has been pointed out this evening by the minister in charge of the resolution that no more berths are available for new ships. I do not belong to Quebec. I have no personal interest in the development of Quebec, except as a Canadian at large, but it has been my privilege to observe the conditions in Quebec at close range during the last few years, and for that matter during the last twenty-five years. What are the conditions prevailing to-day in the port of Quebec? We have reached a point when it is expected that a large portion of the grain of the western part of Canada will be shipped by way of Quebec. It has been represented this evening that it was impossible to ship the grain through Quebec on account of the high freight rates prevailing. We agree that if the rates are maintained at the present level it may not be possible to use the port of Quebec for the export of grain to the extent to which we should use it, but we feel certain that within two or three years a very laTge amount of grain will be carried through the port of Quebec. The works that are contemplated there will spread over four, five or six years. Now, what would be the conditions in western Canada three years hence if we had some forty or fifty million bushels of grain to ship through Quebec and the facilities were not available? I can hear my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), I can hear my hon. friend from Saltcoats (Mr. Sales), and other hon. gentlemen, condemning the powers that be for such a situation. Some hon. gentlemen may say that such a condition will not arise, but others may take the opposite view; it is a matter of opinion. It is a fact that the cattle trade through Quebec has lately increased considerably and it is foreseen even by hon. gentlemen who criticise the resolution that this increase will continue. I do not think there is a man in the House who will contend that the port of Quebec is not to-day marked for a very large export trade in cattle.
Now, my hon. friend (Mr. Sales), whom I always like to hear, to-night presented the minister in charge of the resolution (Mr. Cardin) with this dilemma: he said, which of the two ports will you favour, Montreal or Quebec? But what is the situation as regards the St. Lawrence route? We all know that there is no water highway throughout the world that is comparable with the St. Lawrence, with Montreal at its head, for oceangoing ships. It has been suggested particularly by my hon. friend that it is difficult to understand how such a large amount of money could have been spent between Quebec and Montreal. Well, the maintenance of the St. Lawrence channel between Montreal and Quebec calls for a very large expenditure each year. Why? Because the bottom of the river is not smooth except for a very short distance; and as every hon. gentleman knows, as in the case of every river bed in which there is any great quantity of sand, if dredging operations are not carried out summer after summer the channel must before long be absolutely unfit for use by sea-going vessels. That is why the money is spent on the maintenance of the route between Quebec and Montreal.
I do not think that anyone would for a moment contend that we should close the port of Montreal. I belong to the district of Quebec, and if my own interest in the port of Quebec were at stake I nevertheless would immediately take the ground that it would be altogether unwise in the national interests to close the port of Montreal. It must be kept open as it is to-day; and to keep it open it is necessary to spend the money that is now being spent upon it, even if you increase the debt. Large vessels are coming up the river to-day with Montreal as their destination; and on the St. Lawrence route there are still larger ships that cannot go further than Quebec. And the number of these ships is increasing year by year, so that to-day not another berth is available. And what about Quebec? The question is asked, "If you have so much traffic in Quebec, why do you not pay the interest on the debentures, on the advances that have been made to that port?" That is a proper question. But hon. gentlemen must realize that Quebec is the main immigration port of Canada. What part of Canada during the past twenty-five years has benefited by the immigration that has gone through that port if not western Canada? What benefit has the city of Quebec derived from that large immigration that has favoured our shores? Nothing, practically nothing. The flow of immigration year in and year out during the last thirty or forty years has invariably taken train immediately and made its way towards the fertile plains of the west. That is the situation. A review of the immigration statistics shows that more than
175,000	immigrants have been inspected at the port of Quebec within a year. Last year we inspected about 75,000. Now, this is not a paying proposition; as the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) has pointed out, Mont-

speechtext:
It is exactly because it
is not a new thing that my hon. friend should know about it. Why should he ask me upon what I base my prophecy that the port of Quebec is going to be a great grain exporting port? I base it on that very assumption, that the Transcontinental will be used for transporting grain to the port. I know many hon. gentlemen on the other side, and with respect to freight rates I am simply their pupil, for I do not profess to be an expert on the subject; but I have consulted many men who are in a position, I think, to give an opinion worthy of consideration in this regard, and I have not met one that has not prophesied that the port of Quebec will be a grain exporting port before many years. It is the wish of every hon. gentleman representing western Canada-they have so expressed themselves this evening-that Quebec shall be the natural port for the export of western grain. I thank them for their expression of sympathy with the port. This wish of theirs is going to be realized, and the part of Canada which will profit the most by it will be the west. Thereby the other parts of the Dominion will also profit, because if the great western country is prosperous and
thriving by the expeditious shipping of grain through Canadian ports at reasonable rates, a great agricultural development will follow there. Then who would say for one moment that the rest of Canada is not going to be also prosperous and thriving?
Now, I say both ports are necessary to the development of Canada. I refer only to Montreal and Quebec, Mr. Chairman, because this evening we are confined to a consideration of the St. Lawrence route. Had I an opportunity, I could also say something about the port of Vancouver, the port of St. John and the port of Halifax. But, as I say, our discussion to-night is confined to these two ports, and I repeat, they are necessary and should be developed. If they are developed as we think they should be, not only Quebec and Montreal will profit but the Dominion at large.

Mr. Chairman, I have
no fault to find with the port of Quebec in any way. Indeed, I think the harbour board is to be complimented on their confidence in the port. Certainly if they and the people of Quebec have not confidence in it, it will never amount to what every true Canadian would like to see. But I do take exception to one thing and that is the voting of money year after year to develop the port of Quebec while we are not voting similar assistance to other ports. Let me give an example of what'
I mean. In Vancouver the coastal shipping dues have been trebled as compared with what they were ten years ago to provide money for interest and sinking funds. Has the port of Quebec done that? We cannot bring in a yard of sand or a barrel of lime at Vancouver without paying a tax to the harbour board. Indeed, you can scarcely run a sailing boat into Vancouver without paying a tax. If Quebec would tax those who use their harbour along these lines, would it not be possible for them to pay interest on the money that this government has been advancing for the development of that harbour? I think the government is justly entitled to lend money for the development of the port of Quebec, and that it is in honour bound to pay all the expenses in connection with the immigration sheds and similar accommodation there. I think that the government is also in honour bound to dredge the St. Lawrence up to Quebec to permit the largest ships afloat to reach that port, but federal assistance should stop there, and the harbour board should raise revenue by taxing those who use the [DOT] harbour, to pay interest and other charges, for the development of the harbour.

Quebec Harbour Commissioners

As a member of this House I would be remiss in my duty to those whom I represent if I did not say something in protest against this vote. I do not wish my remarks to be taken as indicating that I object because the vote is given to some other place than Vancouver. My protest is based upon the simple proposition that this is not a business venture. Most of us who went before the people in 1921 told our electors, upon our word as gentlemen and as candidates, that we would come -down here and endeavour to practise economy in our national affairs. Certainly that principle has not been followed in this case. Indeed, the proposal is not based upon the actual business demands either of the port or of the province. We have the figures before us-the minister has given us quite a number; and we have received information from other sources. We know perfectly well that there is no prospect of our ever getting back a cent of principal or interest so far as this advance of $5,000,000 is concerned. We know that because we have the experience in relation to the amount of traffic that goes through the port. We know that $14,000,000 odd have been expended on the port. We know the huge accumulation of arrears of interest. In fact, the information that has been placed before the committee proves beyond reasonable doubt that there is no prospect of revenue from the port in relation either to the existing capital expenditures or to the additional $5,000,000 which the government now proposes to expend there. I submit to the minister and to the members of the government that it is votes of this kind which cause the rank and file, the masses of the people of this country, to look upon the actions of parliament as scandalous. It is votes of this kind that bring parties, governments and parliamentary institutions into contempt before the sensible people of the country.

In 1921, the Board of Railway Commissioners came to Quebec at the request of the harbour commissioners and the board of trade of that city. These public bodies were complaining that the Transcontinental railway was not being put to the best use to which it could be put. They complained that the rates were prohibitive, and that notwithstanding the fact that the Transcontinental railway brought Quebec 214 miles nearer to Winnipeg, with lower grades that enabled a single engine to draw 60 carloads of grain, no grain was shipped over that railway. The public bodies of Quebec were very much interested in seeing that the Transcontinental railway should be used to the best possible advantage with the result that not only would the city and district of Quebec benefit but the western provinces also in whose interest the line had been built. Or is it the desire of the people of Canada that we should proceed to develop our ports and keep Canadian traffic within our own ports? Quebec is one of the oldest ports in Canada. It has a strategic location on the St. Lawrence river. Some years ago the construction of a railway by the people of Canada had the effect of improving that position, and there is no doubt in my mind that if parliament considers this vote favourably it will promote increased trade through the port of Quebec. That increased trade will not merely affect the trade that already goes through the port of Montreal. We have to maintain two sets of harbours on the Atlantic seaboard, Montreal and Quebec during the summer and St. John and Halifax during the winter. Fortunately in western Canada we do not have that condition; our harbours are open the year round. But so far as Quebec is concerned this expenditure was foreseen years ago and money was expended in order that these developments might take place. I think there has been a very unfair criticism to-night from the other side, namely, that the harbour of Quebec was not paying interest on its bonds or on the advances made. Quebec is in a different position from Montreal, in that respect, because you have not the heavy tonnage at Quebec. But the port of Quebec has served a very useful purpose and is serving to-day a useful purpose for the people of Canada, and there is no reason why this vote of $5,000,000 to carry on these developments, to be extended over a period of four or five years, should not be provided. I am satisfied that within the next few years we shall have a western development that will justify the expenditure of this money, and there should be no hesitation on the part of western members to give their support to this measure.

As one of the youngest and most inexperienced members of this House, and knowing the least about the millions of money we hear so much about, I am impelled to say that the people who live in ports on the seaboard and on the lakes must be exceedingly glad for the grain growers and cattle raisers of Canada, because they are the excuse for building needless elevators and dry docks that are never used and harbours
that are#of no use to anybody. Think of the expenditure this year; think of what they are doing in Halifax! What use is to be made of the elevator they are building down there? Then there .is the expenditure at Prince Rupert, improvements in Vancouver- all these tremendous port expansions. They must expect a very great deal of grain to be grown and a tremendous number of cattle to be raised if any of these facilities are to be used at all. As I sit here now in the fourth session since I came to this parliament, I have come to this conclusion that we shall never have economy in Canada until we individually practise economy; until each of us says to his constituents: "If Canada is not to go at once on the rocks"-and anybody who is looking can see that that is the direction in which the country is going-"if it is not to go more rapidly, you and I in this constituency must economize." I offer no apology for voting against this proposal; I feel it is a privilege to do it. I have opposed every expenditure in my riding, even though it has brought me unpopularity to do so. All that the government has been asked by me to spend in Southeast Grey since I came here amounted to $270 a year, and if you knew the trouble I had to get that you would think it was a very large amount indeed. I have not asked for anything, even when my people insisted on it, and in justification to them I must say they did that very seldom. I wonder if we are justified in asking if the request for this immense amount of money does not naturally follow the unpopularity of the proposed subsidy to Sir William Petersen. It is only two or three years ago since we had a vote of almost a similar sum for the same port. I have sat here through almost the whole of this debate and I have not heard any argument that proved to me that additional facilities are needed in Quebec. Five million dollars is a great deal of money to the people who finally pay, and they are the grain growers and cattle raisers of this country. I shall very gladly, Mr. Chairman, oppose this vote.

The hon. member for

If the rate that we think should be granted were given to Quebec and grain began to flow to Quebec, the effect might very well be that a still lower rate as might be given with profit would be given on the lakes. The still further effect of that would be to throw a still greater quantity of grain over the lakes, and we might find that the granting of the lower rate to Quebec would so affect rates on the lakes that further facilities at Quebec would not be required. There is no sentiment in the west as to where our grain should go. It is going to go to that port that offers the best facilities and gives the cheapest rate. The possible effect of that lower rate which we think ought to be granted might be to lower still further the rate on the lakes. rate from being granted over the National Transcontinental. It is, perhaps, more than a suspicion that other railway interests are at work to prevent our grain going in that direction. condition, and I may say that the Cunard line will retain their berth in Quebec, paying fifteen or twenty thousand dollars a year to the commission. They would hardly do that if they had any intention of leaving ,the port entirely.
Now, there is no intention of competing with Montreal. As has been said, vessels of over 15,000 tons cannot go to Montreal; they would never be able to go there if you dug until Domesday. The route to Montreal needs dredging in order to accommodate boats of that tonnage and it would be a physical impossibility for larger vessels to go to that harbour. Let me State the reasons. The water has fallen considerably in the St. Lawrence and in the months of August and September, the drier period of the year, it is not possible for vessels of over 15,000 tons to go up the river to Montreal. This lowering of the water is due as we all know to deforestation; it is clear that as fast as the trees disappear in the upper sources of rivers and lakes the water will flow so much more rapidly in the spring time and will be lower in the summer. That is known to anyone who has had anything to do with the settlement of timber areas.
It stands to reason, too, that when this country is opened and the trees removed the sun would evaporate the water on the surface, so naturally there would be less to flow through the river. The ancestors of most hon. gentlemen, if not the hon. gentlemen themselves, came through the harbour of Quebec. Would they have liked to have had to swim ashore? Are they not .glad rwe gave them a chance to land somewhere? We never charged them for coming in [DOT]-we are glad they came. As has been poffited out by some hon. members on this side, every little parcel pays something to the harbour where it is landed. But the human freight, the immigrant, the man that is to build up our country, the bone and sinew of the Dominion, the man that goes to our western farms and has such a hard time to develop them and make money-he comes through there. We do not want to charge him anything, but we do want to get credit with the government, we want to be allowed at any rate to come before the country and say, "We want those facilities increased, we want to be able to receive immigrants well, and we do not want to be told that in doing that work we are dishonest in not paying.

Some hon. gentlemen opposite say they wish to help the port of Quebec; that they are prepared1 to do anything they can but that they think we have gone the wrong way about it. Instead, they say, of asking for equipment for the development of the port we should have gone to the railway commission or to the government or to somebody and obtained from them an assurance that we would get the benefit of lower freight rates. I think that is stating pretty fairly the position taken by some hon. gentlemen opposite. Well, may I point out to them that this work will take five years, so that we have five years within which to agitate to get the freight rates down?

We have been for a long
time. But twenty years ago my hon. friend's friendls and his party did not exist, and now that they do and they are willing to join with us, there should be a likelihood of our succeeding.
I would point out that the west was very liberally represented in my hon. friend's party at that time, and they failed to get it.

Yes, until they fell away.
At that time they were liberally represented and they were good Liberals, but unfortunately perhaps the situation was not placed before them or was not shown to be as acute as it is to-day. There were other problems to be discussed then, and this one had not become acute.
Surely the hon. member cannot claim it was not acute when the railway was built for the express purpose of delivering our grain and cattle at the port of Quebec.
Well, that was one time the east and the west got together, and we put the thing through. If we get together on this thing we may put the next one over.

It was of very little
use to us to build the road if there was no means of using it afterwards.

Quite so; we are in substantial agreement. Some of my Tory friends say that this is a political matter, well, if it does not go through and I get beaten, any one of them can simply come over here and get elected in my seat. What I was coming at was this; we are about to go over the whole structure of freight rates. We will have five years in which to discuss that. The leader of the Progressives said: "We will not need these things for two of three years more." Well, we will not have them for five years; we will not be able to berth a ship in Quebec until after five years have passed. Surely we will have come to some arrangement in this country for an equitable adjustment of rates before five years. If we have not, the collective wisdom of this country which has been gathered here working on this thing for the last three years, and those who will succeed us, will not mean very much. Indeed, it will be time for a change of government, in the sense not only of a change of the government party in power, but of a change in the system of government. If the people working on this for five years cannot

arrive at a solution satisfactory to the people of Canada, then let us have some kind of dictatorship or something other than parliamentary institutions.
Judging from the direction in which this country is travelling, where are we going to be economically in five years?

We are not so badly off, I think. We are not wealthy, but we are not bankrupt, and we have enormous natural resources. If some of my hon. friends over there will let us use them and make money out of them, we shall be able to pay our debt.
Now, I have taken up three times more time than I should, but I could not let this vote go by without saying a word in an endeavour to convince some of my hon. friends who are sympathetic but who apparently have not grasped all the facts. I am sorry it is not within my power to elucidate the matter further. But I would ask them to give to the matter -the same sympathetic -consideration that we have given to all other projects of the kind placed before us. There has been talk of discrimination in freight rates against Quebec. Do you not think, Mr. Chairman, that there has been discrimination in more than freight rates? We vo-ted for Vancouver; we voted for Toronto; we voted for everywhere else, and never have we heard any such discussion as we have had from the moment the city of Quebec asked -for what is proposed here.

I would like to repeat my question to -the Minister o-f Justice; he did not see fit to answer it when I put it previously. My question was: Did he think it was in the best interests of -this country that we should continue to deepen our waterways and our harbours and build huge canals to satisfy an obsession on the part of the shipping companies to build greater and greater ships, when proof has been given to us this session that the larger boats cannot be operated to-day in competition with the smaller and slower boats? I would like an -answer from the -minister on this -point.
