I do not inflict myself on the House very often, and it will not assist the matter for hon. members opposite to call "Carried." I do not think there has been an item before this House in the last four years so absolutely unjustifiable as the one we are now considering, and I do not think it becomes hon. gentlemen opposite, when they have the whip hand, to call "Carried" and try to choke off hon. members who get up to speak.
Speaking in the House a few nights ago I drew attention to what I felt was an amazing situation, namely, the inflicting upon western wheat growers of elevators all over this country that we were protesting against. I think the government owe us an explanation as to why they are forcing upon us an elevator at Prinlce Rupert, an elevator at Halifax, an elevator at Quebec; and the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Duncan) wants another elevator there. The only answer must be that it is very much more profitable to operate elevators than it is to grow grain. If this vote passes to-night it is just another few nails in the coffin of the present confederation. Is it any wonder that the secession talk is growing in western Canada, when a million and a half people in western Canada have been asking for the opening up of the Hudson Bay route for twenty, twenty-five, even forty years? Who is asking for these elevators that we are called upon to vote money for? We do not want these facilities, but we do want the Hudson bay route. If this vote passes, another 10,000 recruits will be added to the army of secessionists now in western Canada. Discrimination is being practised in this House and in this country to an extent that we people of western Canada are not going to stand for it very much longer. I have in my office and I have received this year a bundle of petitions covering several municipalities with upwards of a thousand names attached to them asking that some steps be made for secession of the western provinces from Canada. I do not know how we can expect anything else when we see the form of justice that is being meted out in this House, because since coming here the only form of justice I have seen is numerical strength. I am sorry to have been forced to make that remark, but it is a fact that the only form of justice applied here is numerical strength. It ill becomes the government of the day to disregard absolutely the protests of hon. members who may not agree with them in matters of this kind. They are 235
simply putting a few more nails in the coffin of the present confederation.

I do not intend to take up much of the time of the House at this late hour after such a lengthy discussion on the port of Quebec, and as on many former occasions it has been my privilege in this House to vindicate the rights of the city of Quebec in regard to the promises made in connection with the development of that port. We have heard many of our Progressive friends state to-night that the port of Quebec should1 be developed and that they were in favour of using that port, but that first we should obtain a reduction in the grain rates. We have also heard the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) state, I think we can assume in the name of his party, that the port of Quebec does not require any additional facilities or development for the present. We may take it for granted that the hon. gentleman does not agree with the declaration made by his late leader and with the moral and legal obligations assumed by the late government towards the city of Quebec. As regards the legal obligation, there was entered into between the government of His Majesty and the city of Quebec an agreement by which, under certain conditions and in view of certain sacrifices made by the citizens of Quebec, the federal government bound itself to develop and improve the port of Quebec in the best interest, not only of the city and province of Quebec, but of Canada as a whole. The city of Quebec handed over to this government property worth more than 83,000,000 for the benefit of the government, of the railway and port facilities in Quebec, on the special consideration that our ports and railway facilities would be developed as promised and agreed to by the late government. Moreover, when we had the honour of receiving in Quebec the former leader of the late government, the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, he announced to the citizens of Quebec that his government had acquired $3,000,000 worth of property along the frontage of the city of Quebec from Sillery to Champlain market; that those properties had been bought by the government in view of developing the port of Quebec, and that that was just the beginning of millions of dollars that the late government proposed to spend in developing that port. What does the present Tory party make of this moral and legal obligation which was assumed by their former leader to develop the port of Quebec? In addition to the numerous arguments that have been



Quebec Harbour Commissioners
advanced to-night in favour of the further development of the port of Quebec, I want to advance especially this legal and moral obligation. It has been stated in this House on many occasions that the government is always willing to fulfil its legal and moral obligations as it intends to do in the Home Bank situation. If this argument holds good in one case, I do not see why the moral and legal obligation towards the city of Quebec should not be fulfilled by this government.
